chapterTitle: Five Words With Understanding — Tongues, Prophecy and Worship That Builds Up
themeTitle: “God Is Not a God of Confusion, but of Peace”

scripture.text: Follow after love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.
scripture.understanding: The bridge from chapter 13. Διώκετε τὴν ἀγάπην — pursue love, chase it, hunt it down; the verb is used for persecution and for running after a prize. Love is the way. And within that way, ζηλοῦτε — be eager for — spiritual gifts, “but especially that you may prophesy.” Love determines which gifts are most to be desired: the ones that build others up.

scripture.text: For he who speaks in another language speaks not to men, but to God; for no one understands; but in the Spirit he speaks mysteries.
scripture.understanding: Speaking in a tongue is directed to God, not to people, because no one ἀκούω — hears, in the sense of understands — what is said. The speaker utters μυστήρια — mysteries — “in the Spirit” (or “in his spirit”). Paul does not despise this. It is real communication with God. But in a gathering, it communicates nothing to anyone else.

scripture.text: But he who prophesies speaks to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.
scripture.understanding: Prophecy, by contrast, speaks to people, and Paul gives the clearest New Testament description of what it does: οἰκοδομή — building up, edification; παράκλησις — encouragement, exhortation, the comfort-word of 2 Corinthians 1; παραμυθία — consolation, gentle comfort, the word used for comforting the grieving. New Testament prophecy is not mainly about predicting the future. It is Spirit-given speech that strengthens, urges and comforts the church.

scripture.text: He who speaks in another language edifies himself, but he who prophesies edifies the assembly.
scripture.understanding: The contrast in one sentence. The tongue-speaker builds up ἑαυτόν — himself. The prophet builds up the ἐκκλησία — the assembly. Paul does not say self-edification is wrong; there is a place for it in private. But in public worship, the test of chapter 12 applies: the gift is given “for the profit of all” (12:7).

scripture.text: Now I desire to have you all speak with other languages, but rather that you would prophesy. For he is greater who prophesies than he who speaks with other languages, unless he interprets, that the assembly may be built up.
scripture.understanding: Paul is not against tongues — “I desire to have you all speak with other languages” — but he wants even more that they would prophesy. The one who prophesies is μείζων, greater — not as a person but in usefulness to the church — than the one who speaks in tongues, “unless he διερμηνεύω — interprets — that the assembly may be built up.” Interpreted tongues build up the church just as prophecy does.

scripture.text: But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking with other languages, what would I profit you, unless I speak to you either by way of revelation, or of knowledge, or of prophesying, or of teaching?
scripture.understanding: Paul puts himself in the scene. If he arrived in Corinth and spoke only in tongues, what would he ὠφελέω — benefit — them? Nothing, unless he brought ἀποκάλυψις (revelation), γνῶσις (knowledge), προφητεία (prophecy) or διδαχή (teaching) — something the mind can receive.

scripture.text: Even things without life, giving a voice, whether pipe or harp, if they didn’t give a distinction in the sounds, how would it be known what is piped or harped?
scripture.understanding: An analogy from music. Even ἄψυχα — lifeless instruments — like the αὐλός (flute, pipe) or the κιθάρα (lyre, harp), must give a διαστολή — a distinction in the notes. A flute that plays random sounds produces noise, not a tune. No one can recognise what is being played.

scripture.text: For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war?
scripture.understanding: A military analogy. If the σάλπιγξ — the war trumpet — gives an ἄδηλος sound, an indistinct signal, who will παρασκευάζω — get ready — for πόλεμος, battle? In ancient armies, different trumpet calls signalled advance, retreat or assembly. An unclear call could get an army killed.

scripture.text: So also you, unless you uttered by the tongue words easy to understand, how would it be known what is spoken? For you would be speaking into the air.
scripture.understanding: The application. Unless your tongue utters εὔσημος — clear, easily recognised — speech, how will anyone know what is being said? “For you would be speaking into the air.” The word is ἀήρ — the same image as the boxer beating the air in 9:26. Unintelligible speech in public worship is a punch that lands on nothing.

scripture.text: There are, it may be, so many kinds of sounds in the world, and none of them is without meaning.
scripture.understanding: There are many γένη — kinds — of φωναί, voices or languages, in the world, and none of them is ἄφωνος — without meaning. Every language communicates to those who know it. Paul's argument rests on the fact that language exists to be understood.

scripture.text: If then I don’t know the meaning of the sound, I would be to him who speaks a foreigner, and he who speaks would be a foreigner to me.
scripture.understanding: If I do not know the δύναμις — the force, the meaning — of the sound, I am a βάρβαρος to the speaker, and he to me. Βάρβαρος was the Greek word for a non-Greek speaker, imitating the “bar-bar” sound of a language you cannot understand. In a city as proud of its Greek culture as Corinth, the word stung. Tongues without interpretation turn brothers into foreigners.

scripture.text: So also you, since you are zealous for spiritual gifts, seek that you may abound to the building up of the assembly.
scripture.understanding: Paul turns their zeal in the right direction. They are ζηλωταί — zealots — for πνεύματα, spiritual manifestations. Fine: then seek to περισσεύω — overflow, abound — in what builds up the church. Paul never tells them to stop being passionate. He tells them where to point their passion.

scripture.text: Therefore let him who speaks in another language pray that he may interpret.
scripture.understanding: Therefore, the one who speaks in a tongue should pray for the ability to interpret. The gift of tongues is not to be suppressed but completed — brought into the service of the whole church.

scripture.text: For if I pray in another language, my spirit prays, but my understanding is unfruitful.
scripture.understanding: If I pray in a tongue, my πνεῦμα — my spirit — prays, but my νοῦς — my mind, my understanding — is ἄκαρπος, unfruitful, barren. Something real is happening in my spirit, but my mind is not engaged, and nobody else benefits.

scripture.text: What is it then? I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also.
scripture.understanding: Paul's conclusion is not either/or but both/and. I will pray with the spirit and with the mind. I will ψάλλω — sing praise, originally to pluck a stringed instrument — with the spirit and with the mind. Christian worship engages the whole person. Mindless emotion and emotionless thought are both less than God deserves.

scripture.text: Otherwise if you bless with the spirit, how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the “Amen” at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say?
scripture.understanding: The practical problem. If you εὐλογέω — bless, give thanks — only in the spirit, how can the ἰδιώτης — the outsider, the ordinary person, the one without this gift — say the ἀμήν at your εὐχαριστία, your thanksgiving? In the synagogue and early church, the congregation answered prayers with a spoken “Amen” — firm, true, I agree. You cannot say Amen to what you do not understand.

scripture.text: For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up.
scripture.understanding: “You most certainly give thanks καλῶς — well.” Paul grants that the tongue-speaker's prayer is genuine and beautiful. “But the other person is not built up.” Good worship is not measured only by what happens between you and God, but also by what happens to your brother.

scripture.text: I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all.
scripture.understanding: A surprising confession that should stop anyone from reading this chapter as anti-tongues. Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them. The apostle is not criticising a gift he lacks. He is regulating a gift he uses more than anyone.

scripture.text: However in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language.
scripture.understanding: “However in the assembly” — that is the decisive qualifier — he would rather speak five words with his νοῦς, his mind, to κατηχέω — instruct, teach; the word gives us catechism — others, than μύριοι, ten thousand, the largest number in Greek, in a tongue. Five against ten thousand. In church, intelligibility wins every time.

scripture.text: Brothers, don’t be children in thoughts, yet in malice be babies, but in thoughts be mature.
scripture.understanding: “Brothers, don’t be παιδία — children — in your φρένες, your thinking.” The fascination with spectacular gifts for their own sake was childish. “In malice, νηπιάζω — be infants” — be innocent of evil like a baby. “But in thoughts be τέλειοι” — mature, grown-up. The same contrast as 3:1–2 and 13:11.

scripture.text: In the law it is written, “By men of strange languages and by the lips of strangers I will speak to this people. Not even thus will they hear me, says the Lord.”
scripture.understanding: Paul quotes Isaiah 28:11–12 — “the law” here means the Scriptures generally. In Isaiah, God warned rebellious Israel that because they would not listen to His prophets in their own language, He would speak to them through the foreign tongue of Assyrian invaders. Unintelligible foreign speech was a sign of judgment on those who refused to hear.

scripture.text: Therefore other languages are for a sign, not to those who believe, but to the unbelieving; but prophesying is for a sign, not to the unbelieving, but to those who believe.
scripture.understanding: Therefore tongues are a σημεῖον — a sign — not to believers but to unbelievers. This is a difficult verse, and verses 23 to 25 explain it. Uninterpreted tongues function as a sign of judgment to unbelievers: they hear only incomprehensible sounds and are confirmed in their unbelief, as in Isaiah's day. Prophecy, on the other hand, is a sign for believers — evidence of God's presence among His people — and, as the next verses show, it can bring unbelievers to faith.

scripture.text: If therefore the whole assembly is assembled together and all speak with other languages, and unlearned or unbelieving people come in, won’t they say that you are crazy?
scripture.understanding: The scenario. The whole church gathers, and everyone speaks in tongues at once. Ἰδιῶται — outsiders, inquirers — or ἄπιστοι, unbelievers, walk in. Will they not say μαίνεσθε — you are mad, raving? Corinth knew the frenzied worship of the pagan mystery cults. A church that looked the same would convince no one.

scripture.text: But if all prophesy, and someone unbelieving or unlearned comes in, he is reproved by all, and he is judged by all.
scripture.understanding: But if all prophesy — in turn, intelligibly — and an unbeliever comes in, he is ἐλέγχω — convicted, exposed, brought under conviction — by all, and ἀνακρίνω — examined, called to account — by all. The intelligible word of God, spoken in the power of the Spirit, does what Jesus said the Spirit would do: convict the world of sin (John 16:8).

scripture.text: And thus the secrets of his heart are revealed. So he will fall down on his face and worship God, declaring that God is among you indeed.
scripture.understanding: The result: the κρυπτά — the hidden things — of his heart become φανερά, exposed. He falls on his face and προσκυνέω — worships — God, ἀπαγγέλλω — declaring openly — that “God is among you indeed.” This echoes Isaiah 45:14, where the nations confess that surely God is in Israel. The goal of Spirit-filled worship is not that visitors say, “What an amazing experience,” but that they say, “God is really here.”

scripture.text: What is it then, brothers? When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, has an interpretation. Let all things be done to build each other up.
scripture.understanding: A precious window into early Christian worship. When you gather, each one has something: a ψαλμός (a song), a διδαχή (a teaching), an ἀποκάλυψις (a revelation), a tongue, an interpretation. Worship was participatory; many members contributed. And the governing rule: πάντα πρὸς οἰκοδομὴν γινέσθω — let everything be done for building up.

scripture.text: If any man speaks in another language, let it be two, or at the most three, and in turn; and let one interpret.
scripture.understanding: Practical regulation for tongues: two, or at most three, ἀνὰ μέρος — in turn, one at a time — and one must interpret. Order, not suppression.

scripture.text: But if there is no interpreter, let him keep silent in the assembly, and let him speak to himself, and to God.
scripture.understanding: If there is no διερμηνευτής — no interpreter — the tongue-speaker should σιγάω, keep silent, in the assembly, and speak to himself and to God. The gift is not forbidden, but in public it must serve the public.

scripture.text: Let the prophets speak, two or three, and let the others discern.
scripture.understanding: Regulation for prophecy: two or three prophets should speak, and the others διακρίνω — weigh, evaluate, discern — what is said. New Testament prophecy is not received uncritically. It must be tested (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). This is a crucial difference from Old Testament prophecy and from Scripture itself: a prophecy in the Corinthian church could be partly right, partly mistaken, and had to be weighed.

scripture.text: But if a revelation is made to another sitting by, let the first keep silent.
scripture.understanding: If a revelation comes to someone sitting nearby, the first speaker should σιγάω — fall silent. No one monopolises the floor, even with a genuine word from God.

scripture.text: For you all can prophesy one by one, that all may learn, and all may be exhorted.
scripture.understanding: All can prophesy, καθ’ ἕνα — one by one — so that all may μανθάνω, learn, and all may be encouraged. The purpose of order is not to restrict the Spirit but to make sure everyone benefits.

scripture.text: The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets,
scripture.understanding: A vital principle: the spirits of the prophets are ὑποτάσσω — subject to — the prophets. The Holy Spirit does not override a person's self-control. Unlike the frenzy of pagan ecstasy, Christian prophecy can wait its turn. “I couldn’t help it; the Spirit made me” is not an excuse for disorder.

scripture.text: for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace, as in all the assemblies of the saints.
scripture.understanding: The theological reason for everything in this chapter: “God is not a God of ἀκαταστασία” — disorder, confusion, chaos, the word used of political upheaval and riots — “but of εἰρήνη,” peace. Worship reflects the character of the God being worshipped. A chaotic God would be worshipped chaotically. The God of peace is worshipped in ordered freedom. “As in all the assemblies of the saints” probably belongs with this sentence, or begins the next.

scripture.text: Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking except in submission, as the law also says,
scripture.understanding: One of the most debated verses in the letter. “Let the wives” — γυναῖκες can mean women or wives; verse 35's “their own husbands” suggests wives — “be quiet in the assemblies.” It cannot mean total silence, because Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5). The most likely meaning, in context, is that wives should not disrupt the weighing of prophecy (v. 29) by questioning or challenging — perhaps their own husbands' prophecies — in public. Σιγάω is the same verb used of the tongue-speaker (v. 28) and the prophet (v. 30): it means stop speaking in a particular situation, not permanent silence. They are to be ὑποτάσσω — in an ordered relationship — “as the law also says,” probably the creation order of Genesis 2.

scripture.text: if they desire to learn anything. “Let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a wife to be talking in the assembly.”
scripture.understanding: If they want to μανθάνω — learn — something, they should ἐπερωτάω — ask, inquire — their own husbands at home. It is αἰσχρόν — disgraceful, in that culture — for a wife to be talking in this way in the assembly. Note: the WEB places the second sentence in quotation marks, reflecting the view of some interpreters that it is a Corinthian slogan which Paul answers in verse 36. Most interpreters read it as Paul's own instruction. Either way, the issue is disruptive questioning during the assembly, not women's participation as such.

scripture.text: What!? Was it from you that the word of God went out? Or did it come to you alone?
scripture.understanding: A sharp double question, aimed at the whole church: did the word of God originate with you, Corinth? Or are you the only ones it has reached? Corinth was acting as if it could make up its own rules for worship, independent of “all the assemblies of the saints” (v. 33). Paul reminds them that they are recipients, not originators, of the word.

scripture.text: If any man thinks himself to be a prophet, or spiritual, let him recognize the things which I write to you, that they are the commandment of the Lord.
scripture.understanding: If anyone thinks he is a προφήτης or πνευματικός — a spiritual person, the very title Corinth prized — let him ἐπιγινώσκω — acknowledge, recognise — that what Paul writes is “the ἐντολή, the commandment, of the Lord.” The test of a true prophet is submission to apostolic teaching. A “spiritual” person who rejects Scripture is not spiritual.

scripture.text: But if anyone is ignorant, let him be ignorant.
scripture.understanding: If anyone ἀγνοέω — ignores, refuses to recognise — this, he is himself not recognised (as the oldest manuscripts read: “he is not recognised,” that is, by God or by the church). The WEB's “let him be ignorant” follows other manuscripts. Either way, the person who rejects apostolic teaching places himself outside it.

scripture.text: Therefore, brothers, desire earnestly to prophesy, and don’t forbid speaking with other languages.
scripture.understanding: The summary. So, brothers, ζηλοῦτε — be eager — to prophesy, and do not κωλύω — forbid — speaking in tongues. Paul refuses both extremes: he will not let tongues dominate the church, and he will not let them be banned. Prophecy is to be pursued; tongues are to be permitted and properly ordered.

scripture.text: Let all things be done decently and in order.
scripture.understanding: The final rule of Christian worship in five words: πάντα εὐσχημόνως καὶ κατὰ τάξιν — everything decently and in order. Εὐσχημόνως — beautifully, fittingly, with dignity. Τάξις — an ordered arrangement, the word used of soldiers in formation or priests serving in their turn (Luke 1:8). Order is not the enemy of the Spirit. It is the shape His freedom takes in a church.

visualMeditations.title: The Trumpet on the Battlefield
visualMeditations.image: Picture a Roman legion drawn up on a plain at dawn, thousands of men in armour waiting for the signal. Every movement of the army is controlled by the trumpet: one call means advance, another means hold, another means retreat, another means form a square. The commander gives the order, and the trumpeter raises his instrument — and blows a confused, wavering, indistinct sound that matches no known call. Down the line, men look at each other. Do we charge? Do we hold? Some move forward, some stay, some turn back. The line breaks. The enemy sees the confusion and attacks.
visualMeditations.meaning: “For if the trumpet gave an uncertain sound, who would prepare himself for war?” Paul's point is that the gathered church needs clear words to be built up, equipped and mobilised. Uninterpreted tongues in public worship, however genuine and beautiful between the speaker and God, are like a trumpet that gives no recognisable call. They do not build up, instruct or encourage anyone else. And the principle applies far beyond tongues. Preaching that is vague, jargon that only insiders understand, worship that is performance without meaning, prayers no one can follow — all of them are uncertain sounds. The church is at war, and its soldiers need clear signals. Five words with understanding are worth more than ten thousand without.

visualMeditations.title: The Visitor Who Fell on His Face
visualMeditations.image: Picture two scenes. In the first, an unbeliever wanders into a house church in Corinth. Everyone is speaking in tongues at once — loud, ecstatic, unintelligible. It reminds him of the frenzied rites he has seen in the temples of Dionysus. He backs out of the door, shaking his head: these people are mad. In the second scene, the same man walks into a different gathering. People are speaking one at a time, in plain Greek, words from God — about sin, about mercy, about the hidden things people carry. And one of them says something that describes exactly what he did last week, something no one could know. His heart is laid bare. He drops to his knees, then to his face, and says, “God is really among you.”
visualMeditations.meaning: Paul's measure of Spirit-filled worship is not how ecstatic it feels but what it does to the people who encounter it. Chaotic tongues confirm an unbeliever in his unbelief. Intelligible prophecy, spoken in the Spirit's power, convicts him, exposes the secrets of his heart and brings him to worship God. That is what Jesus promised the Spirit would do: “convict the world about sin, about righteousness, and about judgment” (John 16:8). The question for every church is not, ‘How spiritual did that feel?’ but, ‘Did anyone meet God?’ The greatest compliment a visitor can pay a church is not, “What a great experience,” but, “God is among you indeed.”

visualMeditations.title: Waiting Your Turn in the Spirit
visualMeditations.image: Picture a gathering where someone is prophesying — a genuine word, delivered with passion. While he is speaking, a woman across the room receives a revelation from God. She does not shout over him. She catches his eye or raises her hand. He finishes his sentence and sits down, and she speaks. Then the elders and others in the room quietly weigh what has been said, testing it against Scripture, holding on to what is good. No one is grabbing the floor. No one claims the Spirit forced him to interrupt. There is freedom, and there is order, and they are not at war with each other.
visualMeditations.meaning: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets, for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace” (vv. 32–33). This is one of the most important principles about the Holy Spirit in the New Testament. Pagan ecstasy overpowered people; the Holy Spirit does not. He works through self-controlled people, and self-control is itself His fruit (Galatians 5:23). That means no one can excuse disorder by blaming the Spirit. It also means prophecy must be weighed (v. 29), because a person speaking under the Spirit's influence can still mix in his own thoughts. Order in worship is not the opposite of the Spirit's freedom. It is the evidence of His presence, because He is the Spirit of the God of peace.

structure.label: Prophecy Builds Up More Than Uninterpreted Tongues (v. 1-5)
structure.body: Pursue love and desire spiritual gifts, especially prophecy; tongues speak to God and build up the speaker, prophecy speaks to people and builds up the church — unless tongues are interpreted.

structure.label: The Need for Intelligibility (v. 6-12)
structure.body: Musical instruments, the battle trumpet and foreign languages all show that sounds without clear meaning communicate nothing; seek gifts that build up the church.

structure.label: Spirit and Mind Together (v. 13-19)
structure.body: Pray for interpretation; pray and sing with spirit and mind; outsiders cannot say Amen to what they do not understand; Paul speaks in tongues more than all, but in church prefers five intelligible words.

structure.label: Tongues, Prophecy and Unbelievers (v. 20-25)
structure.body: Be mature in thinking; uninterpreted tongues function as a sign of judgment to unbelievers, while prophecy convicts them and leads them to worship and confess that God is among you.

structure.label: Order in the Gathering (v. 26-36)
structure.body: Everyone may contribute, but all must build up: two or three tongues in turn with interpretation, two or three prophets with the others weighing; prophets control their own spirits, for God is a God of peace; wives are not to disrupt with questions; the Corinthians are not the source of God's word.

structure.label: The Lord's Command and the Final Rule (v. 37-40)
structure.body: True prophets will acknowledge Paul's instructions as the Lord's command; desire prophecy, do not forbid tongues, and let everything be done decently and in order.

sections.heading: Love Chooses the Gift That Builds Up
paragraphs: Chapter 14 is where Paul applies chapters 12 and 13 to the actual problem in Corinth. And it begins by joining them: “Follow after love, and earnestly desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (v. 1). Love is the way (13:1–13), and love determines which gifts are most to be desired — the ones that build up others most. That is why prophecy is preferred to uninterpreted tongues. Paul's comparison is clear and consistent throughout the chapter: tongues are addressed to God (v. 2), build up the speaker (v. 4) and are unintelligible to others unless interpreted (vv. 2, 5); prophecy is addressed to people and gives them “edification, exhortation, and consolation” (v. 3), building up the church (v. 4).

It is essential to notice that Paul is not against speaking in tongues. “I desire to have you all speak with other languages” (v. 5). “I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all” (v. 18). “Don’t forbid speaking with other languages” (v. 39). Some readers of this chapter have concluded that Paul is quietly trying to eliminate tongues; others have concluded that he wants every believer to practise them publicly. Both readings miss his point. Paul values tongues as genuine communication with God — the speaker “speaks mysteries” “in the Spirit” (v. 2) — and he uses the gift himself. But in the assembly, what matters is whether others are built up. The gathered church is not the place for private devotion that excludes others.

Verse 3 also gives the clearest description of New Testament prophecy anywhere in Scripture: it is speech “to men for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” That is, it builds up, it urges and encourages, and it comforts. It is not primarily prediction, though prediction can be part of it (Acts 11:28; 21:10–11). It is Spirit-prompted speech that applies God's truth to people's lives in a way that strengthens them. And because it is spoken in ordinary language, it engages the mind. Paul's ideal for worship is not mindless ecstasy or spiritless intellectualism, but both together: “I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also. I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also” (v. 15).

sections.heading: Five Words Against Ten Thousand: Why Clarity Is Love
paragraphs: Verses 6 to 19 make one argument from several directions: in public worship, unintelligible speech does not build anyone up. Paul uses analogies the Corinthians would have understood instantly. Musical instruments must make distinct notes or no one can recognise the tune (v. 7). A battle trumpet must sound a clear call or no soldier will know whether to advance (v. 8). A foreign language makes the speaker a βάρβαρος to the hearer, and the hearer a βάρβαρος to the speaker (v. 11) — and in a city proud of its Greek culture, that word meant a foreigner, an outsider, someone whose speech sounded like nonsense. Tongues without interpretation turn brothers and sisters into strangers to one another.

Then verse 16 introduces the ἰδιώτης — the ordinary person, the outsider, the one without this gift. When someone prays or gives thanks only in the spirit, “how will he who fills the place of the unlearned say the ‘Amen’ at your giving of thanks, seeing he doesn’t know what you say?” In early Christian worship, as in the synagogue, the congregation responded to prayers with a spoken Amen — an act of agreement and participation. You cannot say Amen to what you do not understand. Paul grants that the prayer itself may be beautiful: “For you most certainly give thanks well, but the other person is not built up” (v. 17).

And then comes one of the most striking sentences in the chapter: “I thank my God, I speak with other languages more than you all. However in the assembly I would rather speak five words with my understanding, that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in another language” (vv. 18–19). Ten thousand — μύριοι — was the largest number in the Greek language. Five intelligible words outweigh the largest number Paul could name. That is the logic of love. In the gathered church, the question is not, “What edifies me?” but, “What edifies everyone?” And the principle reaches far beyond tongues. Every form of Christian communication — preaching, teaching, singing, praying aloud — should be measured by whether ordinary people can understand it and be built up. Jargon, showmanship and spiritual performance may impress, but they do not edify. Clarity is a form of love.

sections.heading: Ordered Freedom, and the Hard Verses About Wives
paragraphs: Verses 26 to 33 give a precious picture of early Christian worship: “When you come together, each one of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has a revelation, has another language, has an interpretation” (v. 26). Worship was participatory; many members contributed. And Paul regulates that participation without suppressing it. Tongues: two or three, one at a time, with interpretation; if there is no interpreter, silence in public and prayer in private (vv. 27–28). Prophecy: two or three, with the others weighing what is said, and anyone receiving a revelation free to speak while the first gives way (vv. 29–31). The principle beneath it all: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets, for God is not a God of confusion, but of peace” (vv. 32–33). The Holy Spirit does not override self-control. Order is not the enemy of the Spirit. It is the character of the God He reveals.

Verses 34 and 35 are among the most debated in Paul's letters, and honesty requires presenting them carefully. “Let the wives be quiet in the assemblies, for it has not been permitted for them to be talking except in submission, as the law also says, if they desire to learn anything. ‘Let them ask their own husbands at home, for it is shameful for a wife to be talking in the assembly.’” Three things are clear from the context. First, this cannot be a command for women to be completely silent in worship, because Paul has already assumed in 11:5 that women pray and prophesy in the assembly, and he regulates rather than forbids it. Second, the same verb σιγάω (be silent) is used of tongue-speakers without an interpreter (v. 28) and of a prophet when another receives a revelation (v. 30); in each case it means to stop speaking in a particular situation, not to be permanently mute. Third, the immediate context is the weighing of prophecies (v. 29), and the specific issue is wives who want “to learn” by asking questions.

The most likely reading, then, is that Paul is addressing wives who were disrupting the evaluation of prophecy — perhaps by publicly questioning or challenging prophecies, possibly including their own husbands' — and he directs that such questions be asked at home, in keeping with the ordered relationship between husbands and wives grounded in creation (“as the law also says” probably refers to Genesis 2, as in 11:8–9). Some interpreters, following a minority of manuscripts that place these verses after verse 40, argue they were not part of Paul's original letter, but every surviving manuscript includes them. Others, as the WEB's quotation marks suggest, think part of verse 35 is a Corinthian slogan that Paul rejects in verse 36. The strongest reading, consistent with 11:5 and the immediate context, is the first: a specific instruction about disruptive questioning during the weighing of prophecy, not a ban on women's ministry in the gathering. Then Paul turns to the whole church in verse 36: the word of God did not originate with Corinth. They must not invent their own practices. And he closes with the rule that sums up the whole chapter: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (v. 40).

ntConnection.heading: New Testament Connection
paragraphs: The New Testament's first account of tongues, at Pentecost, shows a gift that was immediately intelligible to the hearers: “everyone heard them speaking in his own language” (Acts 2:6), and they said, “we hear them speaking in our languages the mighty works of God!” (Acts 2:11). Even then, some mocked: “They are filled with new wine” (Acts 2:13). Tongues appear again when the Spirit falls on the Gentiles in Cornelius's house, “speaking in other languages and magnifying God” (Acts 10:46), and on the disciples in Ephesus: “they spoke with other languages and prophesied” (Acts 19:6). In each case tongues are a sign of the Spirit's coming. In Corinth, however, they had become a source of pride and disorder, and needed the regulation of love.

Paul's instruction that prophecies must be weighed (v. 29) is echoed in his earliest letter: “Don’t quench the Spirit. Don’t despise prophesies. Test all things, and hold firmly that which is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Notice the balance — do not quench, do not despise, but test. John gives the same instruction: “Beloved, don’t believe every spirit, but test the spirits, whether they are of God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world” (1 John 4:1). The New Testament does not ask believers to choose between openness to the Spirit and discernment. It requires both.

And Paul's vision of worship that engages both spirit and mind, and builds up others, appears again in his later letters. To the Ephesians: “be filled with the Spirit, speaking to one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs; singing, and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Ephesians 5:18–19). To the Colossians: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly; in all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your heart to the Lord” (Colossians 3:16). Notice the phrase “to one another” and “teaching and admonishing one another.” Spirit-filled worship is never merely private. It is the word of Christ dwelling richly in the church and flowing out in ways that build everyone up.

lexicon.strongs: G3619 (verb, build up οἰκοδομέω, oikodoméō, G3618)
lexicon.insight: Strong's defines οἰκοδομή as “architecture, i.e. (concretely) a structure; figuratively, confirmation,” and οἰκοδομέω as “to be a house-builder, i.e. construct or (figuratively) confirm.” The noun and verb together appear seven times in this chapter, making edification its key word. It is the same image as 3:9 (“You are… God’s building”) and 8:1 (“love builds up”). Paul's test for everything that happens in worship is whether it builds up the church — like a builder adding a stone to a wall. Not whether it impresses, not whether it feels powerful, not even whether it is genuine, but whether it makes the whole house stronger. “Let all things be done to build each other up” (v. 26).

Strong's defines προφητεία as “prediction (scriptural or other),” and the verb προφητεύω as “to foretell events, divine, speak under inspiration, exercise the prophetic office.” But the New Testament meaning is broader than prediction. Verse 3 is the key: prophecy speaks to people “for their edification, exhortation, and consolation.” It is Spirit-prompted speech in ordinary language that applies God's truth to people's hearts. Verses 24 and 25 show its power: it can expose the secrets of an unbeliever's heart and lead him to worship. And verse 29 shows its limits: New Testament prophecy must be weighed, because it is spoken by fallible people. It is never placed on the same level as Scripture.

Strong's: “a private person, i.e. (by implication) an ignoramus (compare ‘idiot’).” English gets “idiot” from this word, but in Greek it did not mean stupid; it meant a private individual, a layman, someone without specialised skill. In Acts 4:13 Peter and John are called ἰδιῶται — “unlearned” men without formal rabbinic training. In 14:16 the ἰδιώτης is the person in the assembly without the gift of tongues or interpretation, and in verses 23 and 24 he is an inquirer or newcomer. Paul repeatedly asks the Corinthians to think about this person. Worship must be accessible to the ordinary believer and the curious outsider. If they cannot understand it, they cannot say Amen.

Strong's: “to subordinate; reflexively, to obey.” The word combines ὑπό, under, and τάσσω, to arrange or set in order — the root of τάξις, “order,” in verse 40. It describes being placed in an ordered arrangement. It is used of Christ's willing subjection to the Father (15:28), of the church to Christ (Ephesians 5:24), of believers to governing authorities (Romans 13:1) and of believers to one another (Ephesians 5:21). In verse 32 the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets: the Holy Spirit works through self-control, not by overpowering. Submission in Scripture is not about inferiority of worth; Christ is subject to the Father and fully God. It is about ordered relationships that reflect the God of peace.

Strong's: “instability, i.e. disorder.” The word was used of political turmoil, riots, revolutions and social upheaval. Jesus uses it of the “disturbances” that will precede the end (Luke 21:9), and Paul lists it among his sufferings in 2 Corinthians 6:5 (“riots”). James says “where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion” (James 3:16, using the same word). Paul's point in verse 33 is that worship reflects the God being worshipped. God is not a God of chaos, upheaval and confusion, but of peace. When a church's worship becomes a riot of competing voices, it misrepresents the God it claims to worship. Order is a theological statement.

holySpiritRevelation.intro: The Spirit is dealing with three things in this chapter: the way you measure worship, the people you forget when you minister, and the excuse of spontaneity for what is really disorder.

items.title: Did Anyone Meet God?
items.body: You may have measured worship by how it made you feel. The emotion of the music, the intensity of the moment, the sense of personal blessing. The Spirit wants to give you a different measure: what did it do for others? Did it build up the church? Did the ordinary believer understand it? Did the visitor leave saying, “God is among you indeed”? This is not a call to cold, emotionless worship — Paul prays and sings with the spirit. It is a call to love, which always asks about the other person. Next time you worship, ask not only, “Did I meet God?” but, “Did anyone else meet Him, and did I help?”

items.title: The Person in the Back Row
items.body: Three times in this chapter Paul asks the Corinthians to think about the ἰδιώτης — the ordinary person, the outsider, the newcomer who does not know the language. Who is that person in your world? The new believer who does not understand your church jargon. The visitor who has never been to church. The child, the teenager, the person from a different culture. The Spirit is asking whether your speech, your ministry, your prayers and your worship are clear enough for them to say Amen. Love chooses clarity over display. Five words they can understand are worth more than ten thousand that only impress insiders.

items.title: Is It the Spirit or Is It You?
items.body: “The spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.” It is easy to justify impulsiveness, interruption or disorder by calling it spontaneity or the leading of the Spirit. But the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the God of peace, and self-control is His fruit. He does not override your will; He works through it. The Spirit is asking you to be honest: have you ever used His name to justify your own desire to be heard, to dominate, to be seen as spiritual? True spiritual power waits its turn, submits its words to be weighed, and seeks the good of others. That is not quenching the Spirit. That is walking in step with Him.

audit.title: The Edification Check
audit.body: Think about how you participate in your church — speaking, singing, praying, serving, sharing. Ask: does my participation build up others, or mainly myself? When I speak, are people encouraged, strengthened and comforted? Write down one way your contribution could become more edifying.

audit.title: The Clarity Check
audit.body: Recall the last time you spoke about your faith — in church, at home, to an unbeliever. Did you use words the other person could understand? Did you use jargon or insider language? Could a newcomer have said Amen? Write down one phrase you use that might be unclear to an outsider, and how you could say it more simply.

audit.title: The Self-Control Check
audit.body: Is there any area in your spiritual life where you claim to be led by the Spirit but are actually acting on impulse — interrupting, dominating, refusing correction, insisting your words are from God without allowing them to be weighed? Name it honestly before God.

practices.title: Praying With Spirit and Mind
practices.body: This week, practise verse 15 in your personal prayer. Spend ten minutes praying freely from your spirit — with whatever words, groans, silence or (if you have the gift) tongues come. Then spend ten minutes praying with your understanding: choose a passage of Scripture (Psalm 103 or Ephesians 3:14–21 work well) and pray it back to God phrase by phrase, thinking carefully about each line. Notice how each kind of prayer enriches the other. Do this daily for a week.

practices.title: One Word That Builds
practices.body: Before your next church gathering, pray: “Holy Spirit, give me one word of edification, exhortation or consolation for someone” (v. 3). Then, during or after the gathering, look for the person God puts on your heart, and speak that word to them — simply, clearly, humbly. It may be a verse, an encouragement, a specific thing you have noticed God doing in them, or a gentle comfort. Do not dress it up or claim more authority than it has; let them weigh it. Afterward, write down what happened. This is how prophecy, in its simplest form, builds up the body.

prayerReflection: “Holy Spirit, I want to pursue love above everything. And in that love, I earnestly desire Your gifts — especially the gifts that build up Your people. Thank You for every gift You give: for tongues that speak mysteries to God, for prophecy that strengthens, encourages and comforts, for interpretation, for teaching, for every song and revelation. Teach me to use them not for myself but for the body. Lord, I want to worship You with my spirit and with my mind. I do not want empty emotion or cold intellect. I want both, joined in love. Forgive me for every time my words in Your name have been an uncertain trumpet — unclear, self-focused, impossible for others to understand. Give me five words with understanding rather than ten thousand that impress. Help me to remember the ordinary person, the newcomer, the outsider, and to speak so that they can say Amen. Father, You are not a God of confusion but of peace. Let the worship of Your church reflect who You are. Give me self-control in the Spirit. Let my words be weighed, and let me receive correction humbly. And let every gathering of Your people be a place where unbelievers fall on their faces and say, ‘God is among you indeed.’ Let all things be done decently and in order, for Your glory. In Jesus' name, Amen.”

storyConnections.title: Ezra Reads, and the Levites Give the Sense
storyConnections.summary: After the wall of Jerusalem was rebuilt, all the people gathered as one in the square before the Water Gate, and asked Ezra to bring the book of the law. He stood on a wooden platform and read from early morning until midday, and all the people stood up when he opened the book. Then the Levites moved among the people, reading from the law distinctly and giving the sense, so that they understood the reading. The people wept as they heard it, and Nehemiah told them that this day was holy, and that the joy of the LORD was their strength. They went away to celebrate with great joy, because they had understood the words. That is 1 Corinthians 14 in Israel's history: the word of God, made clear, building up God's people, producing repentance and joy.

storyConnections.title: Pentecost: Every Man in His Own Language
storyConnections.summary: On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came on the disciples like a rushing wind and tongues of fire, and they began to speak in other languages. Jews from every nation heard them declaring the mighty works of God, each in his own language. Some were amazed; others mocked and said they were drunk. Then Peter stood up and preached a clear, intelligible sermon about Jesus crucified and risen. The people were cut to the heart and asked what they should do, and about three thousand believed and were baptised that day. Tongues drew a crowd and signalled the Spirit's arrival; plain prophetic preaching brought conviction and conversion. Pentecost shows both gifts in their proper places, and Paul's teaching in 1 Corinthians 14 keeps them there.

storyConnections.title: A Foreign Tongue at the City Wall
storyConnections.summary: Through Isaiah, God warned the leaders of Jerusalem that because they mocked His prophets' plain message, He would speak to them through people of strange lips and a foreign tongue. That warning came true when the Assyrian army came to Jerusalem's walls. The Assyrian commander, the Rabshakeh, shouted his threats to the people on the wall. Hezekiah's officials begged him to speak in Aramaic, the diplomatic language the common people did not understand, rather than in the Judean language. Foreign speech at the wall was the sound of judgment on a nation that had refused to listen to God's clear word. Paul quotes Isaiah 28 in 1 Corinthians 14:21 to explain why uninterpreted tongues do not help unbelievers: unintelligible speech is a sign of judgment, not a means of conversion. God's preferred way to save is a clear word.
